source: Schoenfeld (1992) Learning to think mathematically: problem solving, metacognition, and sense-making in mathematics (Handbook of Research on Mathematics Teaching and Learning, pp. 334-370)
finding: The core critique of Polya: his heuristics were descriptive, not prescriptive. They let you recognise a strategy once used, but did not give enough detail for someone unfamiliar with the strategy to carry it out.
numbers: Not a quantitative claim. Example given: 'examine special cases' is one label, but three worked problems need three different, unrelated special-case procedures.
quote: the characterizations of them were descriptive rather than prescriptive
limits: Schoenfeld's own reading and a review chapter, not an experiment. He adds that the evidence had 'turned in Polya's favor' over the prior decade once strategies were specified in finer detail.
agent_relevance: A menu entry like 'specialise' is too vague to act on. Each operator in the schema (O1 to O8) needs a concrete procedure and a stated trigger, or the model will only produce its label.

source: Schoenfeld (1992) Learning to think mathematically (section: Making heuristics work)
finding: The worked case of one Polya heuristic splitting into many. Problem 1 (closed form of a sum with integer n): try n=1,2,3 and find a pattern, then prove by induction. Problem 2 (roots of a polynomial and its reversed-coefficient twin): try easily factorable polynomials, NOT n=1,2,3, which is a wild goose chase. Problem 3 (recursive sequence a_n = mean of previous two): choose starting values 0 and 1 and draw the picture.
numbers: Three problems, three different special-case strategies. Schoenfeld says one could list 'a dozen more' at this grain for specialising alone, and the same holds for almost all Polya strategies.
limits: Illustrative, hand-picked problems. No success rates attached.
agent_relevance: Specialise (O1) needs preconditions keyed to problem class (integer parameter, polynomial roots, recursive sequence). Our S9 record of 'operator that solved a subgoal plus problem class' is the right data structure for learning these preconditions.

source: Schoenfeld (1992) Learning to think mathematically (summary of pre-1980 heuristics-teaching studies: Wilson 1967, Smith 1973, Kilpatrick 1967, Kantowski 1977, Lucas 1974, Harvey and Romberg 1980, Begle 1979)
finding: Through the 1970s there was little empirical support that teaching Polya-style heuristics improved problem solving. Taught heuristics did not transfer to new domains (Wilson 1967, Smith 1973). Heuristic use correlated with test performance but only weakly (Kantowski, Kilpatrick, Lucas). A dissertation compilation called the teaching 'promising' but unproven (Harvey and Romberg 1980).
numbers: No pooled numbers given. Begle (1979) is quoted: strategies are 'both problem- and student-specific', so teaching one or few strategies to all students is 'far too simplistic'.
limits: Second-hand summary by an author who argues for a particular fix (finer-grained strategies plus control). Effects were measured on human students over short courses.
agent_relevance: Supports G1 and the 'not a fixed menu' stance: a flat list of heuristics offered to every problem has weak support. Selection must depend on problem and solver state.

source: Schoenfeld (1992) quoting Newell on Polya and AI, and Hunt (1975)
finding: AI researchers revered Polya but did not build on him because the work seemed too informal. Newell: 'Polya revered and Polya ignored'. Hunt (1975): Polya gives ad hoc examples but no general rules. Schoenfeld notes the 1980s were kinder to Polya-style heuristics once AI-style fine-grained analysis was applied (Heller and Hungate 1985, Rissland 1985).
numbers: None.
limits: Quoted second-hand. The original Newell paper (The heuristic of George Polya and its relation to artificial intelligence, 1981 to 1983 depending on citation) was not reachable this session.
agent_relevance: Our schema is exactly the step AI skipped: turning Polya operators into procedures with triggers that code can check (S6 impasse, typed operator, test result).

source: Schoenfeld (1992) Learning to think mathematically (section: Self-regulation; reports Schoenfeld 1985, 1987 college problem-solving course)
finding: The key finding that heuristics need control. In a collection of more than 100 videotapes of college and high-school students on unfamiliar problems, about 60% of attempts were 'read, decide quickly, pursue that direction regardless' with no check on progress. After his problem-solving course, fewer than 20% of attempts were of that type, with a concomitant rise in success. A mathematician solving a hard problem spent more than half his time just making sense of the problem and commented explicitly on progress several times.
numbers: About 60% before the course, under 20% after. Collection size more than 100 tapes. Time-line graphs for one student pair (20 min no progress check), one mathematician, one post-course pair (dropped two bad paths, one after 8.5 min).
limits: Descriptive time-line data; Schoenfeld gives no sample sizes, test statistics or control group for the 60% and 20% figures in this chapter. Students also learned from many other course features.
agent_relevance: Strongest argument for G1/S6: the failure was not missing heuristics but never stopping a failing path. Our program-level progress and impasse detector plays the role of the instructor's roving questions.

source: Schoenfeld (1992) Learning to think mathematically (description of the course intervention)
finding: The control intervention was three questions asked by an instructor at any time during group work: What exactly are you doing? Why are you doing it? How does it help you? Students at first could not answer, then began to pre-empt the questions, and the habit became automatic by term end.
numbers: About one third of class time spent in small groups; 'the better part of a semester' needed for the change.
quote: What (exactly) are you doing? ... Why are you doing it? ... How does it help you?
limits: One teacher, one course; no controlled comparison of the three questions alone. Slow to acquire in humans, which may not apply to a model that can be prompted every step.
agent_relevance: A cheap, code-triggerable check for S4/S6: at each major step the program asks the model to state what, why, and expected use of the output. Needs testing against G10 (reasoning text is not evidence); use the answer only to decide whether to abandon, with code checking real output.

source: Lester, Garofalo and Kroll (1989) as summarised in Schoenfeld (1992): metacognition instruction in seventh-grade mathematics
finding: A classroom intervention where the teacher acts as external monitor, models good executive behaviour and discusses strategies (guess and check, working backwards, looking for patterns). Main conclusions: control and concept understanding develop together; gains need many varied problems over a long period; metacognition teaching works best inside a specific domain; the teacher finds it hard to keep the monitor role when students lack basics.
numbers: 16.1 hours over 12 weeks, 35.7% of mathematics class time; two seventh-grade classes (one regular, one advanced).
limits: Read only through Schoenfeld's summary. No effect sizes reported in that summary.
agent_relevance: Supports domain-specific operator preconditions and against generic prompts. Also warns that a monitor role degrades when basics are weak, matching G12 (search only where there is a foothold).

source: Schoenfeld (1992) Learning to think mathematically (sections on school problem-solving instruction and on fine-grained strategies; Silver 1979, 1981; Heller and Hungate 1985)
finding: When textbooks drill a heuristic (show it, practise it, test it), it stops being a heuristic and becomes an algorithm. Detailed studies show 'exploiting related problems' is far more complex than it appears (Silver). Heller and Hungate's recipe for teaching problem-solving strategies: make tacit processes explicit, get students talking, guided practice, learn component procedures well, stress qualitative understanding plus specific procedures.
numbers: None.
limits: Opinion plus literature summary.
agent_relevance: A warning for a fixed operator menu: the value is in knowing when to apply, not the label. Keep the operator application inside an impasse (G1) and record which problem features it fit.

source: Schoenfeld (1979) Explicit heuristic training as a variable in problem-solving performance, JRME 10, 173-178; revised as Schoenfeld (1985) Mathematical Problem Solving, ch. 6; described here from Rott and Gawlick (2014)
finding: The founding controlled test of Polya-style heuristics. Seven students were randomly split into an experimental group (4) and a control group (3). Both did a 5-problem pretest, then five individual training sessions of four problems over two weeks, then a 5-problem posttest. Both groups saw identical worked solutions. The experimental group also got a list of five heuristics and solutions overlaid with notes on which heuristic was used and how. Heuristics were: draw a diagram; look for an inductive argument if there is an integer parameter; argue by contradiction; consider a similar problem with fewer variables; set subgoals.
numbers: N=7 (4 vs 3). No student solved more than 2 pretest problems. After training the control group did not improve on average; the experimental group solved on average 2 more problems than at pretest. Pretest problems 20 min each. Training problems: solution shown after at most 15 min. Posttest had a 5-minute warning prompting a rethink.
quote: the students in the heuristics group saw in addition an overlay to each solution
limits: The Schoenfeld original (JRME 1979 PDF) could not be opened this session; these numbers come from Rott and Gawlick's description. Tiny N, no statistics, no no-training group. Tests were chosen so each problem suits one trained heuristic.
agent_relevance: The best human evidence that naming a heuristic and annotating how it was used in worked examples beats plain examples. Maps to storing S9 look-back notes that tag the operator and how it was applied, then showing those as examples.

source: Rott and Gawlick (2014) Explizites oder implizites Heurismentraining: was ist besser? (critique of Schoenfeld 1979)
finding: Lists the weaknesses of the original: only 7 participants, no group that took just the tests, so test difficulty and the training effect cannot be separated; the five heuristics differ widely in scope; problem order differed between groups; 5-minute warnings added in the posttest may have helped one group more; heuristic use was measured only indirectly via fully solved problems. They note there were no comparable quasi-experimental studies since 1979, a point Sweller (1990) also made.
numbers: n=7 in the original.
limits: Written by replicators. German-language paper (translated by the reader of this file).
agent_relevance: Tells us how thin the base is: the central human result for explicit heuristic teaching rests on 7 people plus one small replication. Treat all heuristic-menu claims as [S] status.

source: Rott and Gawlick (2014) Explizites oder implizites Heurismentraining: was ist besser? (results of the replication under improved conditions)
finding: Replicated the direction of Schoenfeld's result with a no-training comparison group. Explicit heuristic training (list plus margin notes on worked solutions) beat identical practice with worked solutions alone, and practice alone beat no training. The practice-only group's own gain was not significant.
numbers: German student teachers: explicit group n=9, practice-only n=10, no-training n=9. ANCOVA on group with pretest covariate F=6.593, p=0.005. Explicit group improved about 4 raw points (about half a problem); practice-only group slightly decreased; no-training group fell about 4 points (pretest 16 total vs posttest 12 total, so the posttest was harder). Corrected effect sizes d: explicit vs practice-only 0.786, explicit vs no-training 1.438, practice-only vs no-training 0.640. Explicit vs practice-only posttest Bonferroni p=0.043. Within-group gain for explicit group t=-2.626, p=0.015, d'=0.88; practice-only t=0.391 n.s. Gain difference explicit vs practice-only t=2.423, df=17, p<0.05.
limits: About 10 per group, volunteers from one lecture, mathematics teacher students (strong maths background). Only 3 training sessions with 15 problems (3 per strategy). Tests were not equally hard. Matching of pairs failed (only five pairs left), so groups were unmatched. Heuristic use itself was not coded, only scores. Outlier check did not change significance.
agent_relevance: Good size-of-effect anchor (d about 0.8 on trained heuristics, very short training) for how much naming heuristics helps on problems built to suit them. Do not expect this size on arbitrary problems.

source: Rott and Gawlick (2014) design of the replication (choice of heuristics and training materials)
finding: The replicators changed the heuristic set to: draw a figure, consider special cases, work backwards, drop a condition, consider similar problems with fewer variables. They dropped Schoenfeld's induction and contradiction as too domain specific and subgoals as too general. Explicit group got a three-quarter A4 page listing the five heuristics and margin boxes in the solutions pointing out their use.
numbers: One test problem and one training problem per heuristic in each session; 5 training problems per session over 3 sessions; tests of 5 problems with 90 minutes allowed.
limits: Even the revised set still varies a lot in breadth: the replicators say 'fewer variables' is much more restricted than 'draw a figure' or 'work backwards'.
agent_relevance: The five here are close to our O1, O2, O4, O5 plus 'draw a figure' (our O6 change representation). Confirms the schema operator set matches what was trainable in humans; also confirms breadth differs, so O5 and O6 may be usable more often than O1.

source: Rott and Gawlick (2014) literature review of heuristic training studies (Lucas 1974, Kantowski 1977, Koichu, Berman and Moore 2007, Collet 2009, Brockmann-Behnsen 2012)
finding: Most heuristic-training studies gave weak results (citing Schoenfeld 1992). Lucas (1974) compared explicit vs implicit training and found a slight advantage for explicit. Kantowski (1977) trained only explicitly. Koichu, Berman and Moore (2007): five-month field experiment in two Israeli grade-8 classes, amount of heuristic use correlated with learning gain, but no control group. Collet (2009, PROSA project, grades 7 and 8): more heuristics used after training, medium significant correlation between heuristic use and success. Brockmann-Behnsen (2012, 2014): first results in four grade-8 classes favour explicit over implicit training.
numbers: Per the paper's footnotes: Lucas, 30 university students, 8 weeks, two groups, one given extra explicit heuristic information; Kantowski, 8 ninth-graders trained over several months on geometric proofs. A web search snippet describes Lucas as 13 weeks, so the duration is inconsistent between secondary sources.
limits: Second-hand. Several of these confound heuristic teaching with self-regulation training or with teacher quality.
agent_relevance: Consistent pattern: explicit labelling gives a modest edge, correlation of heuristic use with success is medium, and causal evidence is thin.

source: Schoenfeld (1985) Mathematical Problem Solving (book; four-part framework, chapter 7 on explicit heuristic training), cited in a 1989 dissertation
finding: The framework has four parts: resources, heuristics, control, beliefs. A later dissertation cites it for the point that heuristic-teaching studies gave disappointingly inconsistent results, which Schoenfeld and others attributed largely to ignoring metacognition.
numbers: Not read. Only search-result snippets seen.
limits: The book and the dissertation text were not opened. Treat as pointer only.
agent_relevance: Pointer to read next: chapters 4 to 7 of the book for the original protocol evidence and the full heuristic-training analysis.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Plan-and-Solve Prompting: Improving zero-shot chain-of-thought reasoning by large language models (ACL 2023)
finding: A Polya-like 'devise a plan, then carry it out' trigger sentence beats the plain 'let's think step by step' trigger in zero-shot GPT-3. Adding two detail instructions (extract relevant variables and numbers; calculate intermediate results; pay attention to calculation) gives PS+, which helps more.
numbers: text-davinci-003, zero-shot accuracy (%): Zero-shot-CoT / PS / PS+ . MultiArith 83.8 / 87.2 / 91.8. GSM8K 56.4 / 58.2 / 59.3. AddSub 85.3 / 88.1 / 92.2. AQuA 38.9 / 42.5 / 46.0. SingleEq 88.1 / 89.2 / 94.7. SVAMP 69.9 / 72.0 / 75.7. Average over six: 70.4 / 72.9 / 76.7. Few-shot manual-CoT average 77.6. CommonsenseQA 65.2 (zero-shot CoT) vs 71.9 (PS+). StrategyQA 63.8 vs 65.4. Last-letter 64.8 vs 75.2. Coin flip 96.8 vs 99.6. Zero-shot-CoT with self-consistency reached 70.7 on GSM8K and 81.7 on SVAMP; PS+ with self-consistency was higher on both. Few-shot comparisons use 8 examples.
limits: One old model (GPT-3 davinci-003); gains on GSM8K are small (2.9 points for PS+). The planning gain on strong modern models is not shown here. The PS+ gain comes mostly from the extra detail instructions, not from the plan alone (PS alone is only +1.8 on GSM8K).
agent_relevance: A plan-first prompt is a cheap, weak gain; mostly it changes error type. Keep a short plan in S1/S2 but do not count it as the source of accuracy.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Plan-and-Solve Prompting, error analysis section
finding: Planning reduced two error types but left the third unchanged. Understanding errors (semantic misunderstanding) were not helped by a plan.
numbers: 100 sampled GSM8K problems, error share of all problems: calculation errors / missing-step errors / semantic misunderstanding: Zero-shot-CoT 7% / 12% / 27%; PS 7% / 10% / 26%; PS+ 5% / 7% / 27%. Incorrect problems out of 100: CoT 46, PS 43, PS+ 39. Of 100 PS outputs sampled, 90 actually contained a plan. Variable definitions and plan presence correlate negatively with calculation and missing-step errors.
limits: Hand classification by authors on a sample; different counts of wrong answers across methods. Understanding errors (the largest class at 27%) did not move.
agent_relevance: Matches Polya step 1 (understand) being the bottleneck: planning prompts do not fix misreading. S1 UNDERSTAND needs its own check (restate, then verify against the text) rather than relying on a plan prompt.

source: Zheng et al. (2023) Take a Step Back: Evoking reasoning via abstraction in large language models (Step-Back Prompting)
finding: A Polya generalise step: first ask a more abstract question ('what principles are involved?'), then answer using them. It helped on physics and chemistry with PaLM-2L and GPT-4, but its edge over plain chain-of-thought was small for the stronger model.
numbers: MMLU high-school physics / chemistry, mean of 5 runs. PaLM-2L baseline 66.4 / 70.9; +CoT 65.0 / 75.3; +Step-Back 73.2 / 81.8. GPT-4 baseline 69.4 / 80.9; +CoT 82.9 / 85.3; +Step-Back 84.5 / 85.6. Llama2-70B baseline 51.9 / 55.7; +CoT 59.3 / 64.1; +Step-Back 64.8 / 66.7. Few-shot exemplars: robust from 1 to 5. The abstract reports up to +27% on TimeQA and +7% MuSiQue over PaLM-2L.
limits: Gains against zero-shot CoT are small for GPT-4 (physics +1.6, chemistry +0.3, within run noise of about 1.2). Tasks are knowledge and principle recall heavy, not proof problems. On GSM8K the authors say retrieving principles first is not needed.
agent_relevance: Supports O2 (generalise) mainly as 'retrieve the governing principle first'. For a strong model the benefit over CoT is near the noise level, so use only at impasse or on knowledge-heavy classes.

source: Zheng et al. (2023) Step-Back Prompting, error analysis
finding: Abstraction itself rarely fails; the reasoning that follows is the bottleneck. Step-back fixes some baseline errors but breaks others.
numbers: On MMLU physics (PaLM-2L): Step-Back corrects 20.5% of baseline errors while introducing 11.9% new errors. More than 90% of Step-Back's remaining errors occur in the reasoning step, only a small fraction in the principle-retrieval step. TimeQA: more than half of remaining errors are reasoning errors and 45% come from retrieval failing even with a good step-back question. Abstract: fixes up to 40% of base errors, introduces at most 12%.
limits: Error taxonomy assigned with model help and hand review; breakdown shown only on selected tasks.
agent_relevance: The 20.5% fixed vs 11.9% broken pair is a template: any operator should be reported as fixed-versus-broken rates, and our G2/G3 checks must catch the broken cases.

source: Zhou et al. (2023) Least-to-Most Prompting Enables Complex Reasoning in Large Language Models (ICLR 2023)
finding: Polya 'decompose and solve auxiliary problems in order' implemented as two prompts: first list the simpler sub-questions, then answer them in sequence, each answer feeding the next. Large gains on generalising to harder problems than shown in the exemplars.
numbers: SCAN length split with code-davinci-002: standard prompting 16.7%, chain-of-thought 16.2%, least-to-most 99.7%. text-davinci-002: 6.0 / 0.0 / 76.0. code-davinci-001: 0.4 / 0.0 / 60.7. Only 13 failures remained: 6 misread 'twice/thrice' after 'around', rest misread 'after' as 'and'. Last-letter concatenation, list length 4 to 12: CoT 84.2 falls to 31.8; least-to-most 94.0 falls to 74.0. CoT with 4 or 8 independent exemplars on length 12 reached only 37.4 and 38.4.
limits: SCAN and symbolic tasks are very regular and decompose cleanly; the authors say decomposition prompts are domain-specific and do not transfer across domains. Needs hand-written decomposition exemplars.
agent_relevance: Strong evidence for O3 (decompose) where structure is compositional. Weak transfer across domains argues for storing the decomposition exemplar per problem class (S9).

source: Zhou et al. (2023) Least-to-Most Prompting, math word problem results (GSM8K and DROP)
finding: On ordinary grade-school maths the decomposition gain is small, and for easy two-step problems chain-of-thought was better. The edge shows up only on longer problems.
numbers: code-davinci-002 accuracy: GSM8K zero-shot 16.38, standard 17.06, CoT 60.87, least-to-most 62.39. DROP (numerical subset) non-football: CoT 74.77 vs L2M 82.45; football: CoT 59.56 vs L2M 73.42. GSM8K by required steps (L2M vs CoT): 2 steps 74.53 vs 76.68; 3 steps 68.91 vs 67.29; 4 steps 59.73 vs 59.39; 5 or more steps 45.23 vs 39.07.
limits: 1.5 point overall GSM8K gain on one model is within plausible noise; single prompt per method. Gains concentrate where problems exceed exemplar length.
agent_relevance: Decompose only when the problem is long (at or above about 4 steps) or fails a first attempt. On short problems it can lose. Supports using step count as a precondition for O3.

source: Zhou et al. (2024) Self-Discover: Large language models self-compose reasoning structures (ICML)
finding: A heuristic menu applied by the model: 39 reasoning modules (taken from Fernando et al. 2023) are offered, and the model does three meta-prompt steps once per task: SELECT useful modules, ADAPT them to the task, IMPLEMENT them as a JSON-like reasoning plan, then solves each instance by filling in the plan. Large gain on tasks needing world knowledge or agent reasoning; small gain on maths.
numbers: Accuracy PaLM 2-L: direct / CoT / Plan-and-Solve / Self-Discover. BBH (23 tasks) 56% / 60% / 61% / 67%. T4D 30% / 40% / 42% / 69%. MATH (200 sampled) 45% / 42% / 49% / 50.5%. GPT-4: BBH 58 / 75 / 73 / 81; T4D 51 / 52 / 53 / 85; MATH 70.5 / 71 / 70 / 73. Self-Discover beat direct on 23 of 25 tasks and CoT on 21 of 25 (PaLM 2-L). Uses 10 to 40 times fewer inference calls than self-consistency style baselines. On MATH, 74.7% of failures were computation errors, not wrong reasoning structure.
limits: Gains on MATH are 1 to 3 points over Plan-and-Solve and well within noise for 200 problems. Benchmarks other than MATH are not proof-style. Per-task structure still comes from the same model that makes the errors (G4, G10 apply).
agent_relevance: The cheapest form of a menu works: one up-front structure per problem class, not per attempt. The 74.7% computation-error finding says most maths failures are execution, which code can check (G2, G3).

source: Lee et al. (2026) Llama-Polya: Instruction tuning for large language model based on Polya's problem-solving (arXiv 2602.10597)
finding: An 8B model was fully fine-tuned on synthetic tutoring dialogues (derived from GSM8K) structured by Polya's four steps: understand, plan, carry out, look back. The paper evaluates tutoring behaviour, not solve rate. General instruct and base models skipped the stages and gave the answer in one turn; the math-and-Polya tuned models spread the dialogue across stages.
numbers: Llama-3.1-8B variants: base, instruct, polya-v2, metamath, metamath+polya-v2. Stage-annotation 'error rates' polya-v2 0.0%, metamath 0.4%; base and instruct higher, and the sequentially tuned metamath+polya-v2 also had high error rates (authors suspect interference). Instruct model stage mix about 26/19/33/23% across the four stages. Six maths education experts: self-level feedback 4.22/5, task-level feedback 2.8 to 3.2/5. Evaluation across arithmetic, measurement and geometry.
limits: Tutoring dialogue, not accuracy. Six expert raters; annotation by authors. Synthetic training data. The model rarely returned to earlier stages when conceptual gaps persisted, the authors note. No comparison with a plain prompt of the Polya steps.
agent_relevance: Shows an LLM can follow the Polya step order when trained, but offers no evidence that doing so raises correct answers. Do not cite as support for accuracy gains.

source: Anonymous authors (2026) SHAPE of Thinking: Mathematical heuristics for analyzing and improving LLM reasoning (arXiv 2608.28600), framework and annotation reliability
finding: A fixed 11-family heuristic taxonomy built from Polya, Koichu et al. (2007), Favier and Posamentier and Krulik, used to label each content unit of a model's chain of thought. Families: change of representation, cognitive reinterpretation, symbolic formalisation and auxiliary elements, problem classification/rephrase, wishful thinking (simplify/reduce), explicit case analysis/decompose, contradiction, analogy/related theorems, experimental and pattern exploration, working backward, verification and looking back; plus a non-heuristic class.
numbers: Gold standard: 48 trajectories, 7,565 sentences, 1,598 content units, consensus-labelled by four authors. Best automated annotator Grok-4.1-Fast: F1 77.16, Gwet AC1 0.909. Qwen3.5-27B (default, open): F1 70.44, AC1 0.894. Others F1 65 to 72. Annotating 445 trajectories with Grok cost about $100.
limits: Annotator is an LLM; F1 of 70 to 77 means labels are noisy. Labelling observable text, not internal computation (the authors acknowledge faithfulness issues). Authors are not named in the HTML text I read.
agent_relevance: A ready, human-validated coding scheme for our logs (adjacent to ThinkARM episode analysis, which is another subfield). Use it to count which Polya moves our agent actually emits in S3 to S6.

source: SHAPE of Thinking (2026), MATH-Perturb analysis
finding: When a problem is changed so that a different solution approach is needed, accuracy drops and the mix of heuristics used changes more than for a harmless rewording. So models do shift strategies when needed, but not enough to keep accuracy.
numbers: Pass@1 original / simple perturbation / hard perturbation (%): Qwen3-8B 96.0 / 94.0 / 84.0; Qwen3-32B 92.0 / 90.0 / 76.0; Nemotron-Cascade-8B 92.0 / 95.0 / 71.0; Olmo-3-7B-Think-RLVR 97.0 / 94.0 / 76.0; Qwen2.5-7B SimpleRL-Zoo 61.7 / 58.3 / 31.3; Qwen2.5-14B SimpleRL-Zoo 67.0 / 69.6 / 40.9. Heuristic-frequency Jensen-Shannon divergence from original: simple .043 to .197, hard .066 to .253; hard greater than simple for all six models in a one-sided Wilcoxon test (uncorrected p<.05).
limits: Six models, MATH-Perturb only, uncorrected tests, labels from an LLM annotator. Divergence shows change in heuristic mix, not that the change was right.
agent_relevance: Supports the claim that failure on novel variants is a control problem (not switching approach enough). A code-side impasse trigger plus operator choice (S6) addresses this directly.

source: SHAPE of Thinking (2026), mode-seeking of RLVR in heuristic space
finding: Successful solutions from RL-trained models overlap heavily with heuristic profiles already seen in their base model, consistent with RL concentrating on existing strategies rather than inventing new ones. Unrelated base models do not overlap.
numbers: Density / Coverage of RL solutions inside base-model neighbourhoods (k=3, cosine): Qwen3-1.7B-Base to GRPO 1.219 / 0.871; Olmo-3-7B to Think-RL-Zero 1.250 / 0.707; Qwen2.5-7B to SimpleRL-Zoo 1.511 / 0.888; DeepSeek-Math-7B to SimpleRL-Zoo 1.525 / 0.950. Cross-model baselines 0.594 / 0.348 and 0.525 / 0.437.
limits: Successful trajectories only on MATH-Perturb; neighbourhood size sensitivity reported in the appendix, not checked here.
agent_relevance: Prompted heuristics can only pull out strategies the base model already holds, so a menu may help selection but cannot add skills. Consistent with G12 (search lifts only where there is a foothold).

source: SHAPE of Thinking (2026), Heuristic-Augmented Plan-GRPO
finding: Putting the 11 heuristic families in the training rollout prompt (the model names a relevant heuristic and why it applies before each major step) beat a plain planning prompt in RL training. The evaluation prompt contained no heuristic guidance, so the gain is a trained-in effect, not a prompt-time effect.
numbers: Three models (DeepSeek-Distill-Llama-8B, Qwen3-1.7B-Base, Qwen3.5-4B-Base), three seeds, trained on MATH train split, evaluated on MATH-Perturb original/simple/hard, MATH500 and Minerva. HA-Plan-GRPO improved Avg@16 in 14 of 15 model-by-test comparisons and Pass@16 in 14 of 15. Mean gains 1.1 to 7.0 points Avg@16 and 0.4 to 2.4 points Pass@16. Largest: DeepSeek-Distill-Llama-8B mean Avg@16 42.8% to 49.8%, Pass@16 69.7% to 72.1%.
limits: Training-time intervention; says nothing about prompting a frozen model. Authors' own method and benchmark framing; three seeds. The comparison arm is planning-only, so the gain is the heuristic list over a plan, not over plain prompting.
agent_relevance: The only controlled LLM result found where a Polya-style heuristic menu adds to a plan. Hints the menu helps when selection is reinforced by reward; for a fixed model we must test it ourselves at equal tokens (G7).

source: Koichu, Berman and Moore (2007) Heuristic literacy development and its relation to mathematical achievements of middle school students (Instructional Science), as summarised in Rott and Gawlick (2014)
finding: A five-month field intervention in two grade-8 classes in Israel, delivered through teachers working with researchers who built a shared 'heuristic vocabulary'. The amount of heuristic use correlated positively with learning gain on an SAT-style measure. There was no control group.
numbers: Numbers not read (second-hand description only).
limits: Original paper not opened. Correlational. Teacher-mediated.
agent_relevance: Gives the human version of a 'heuristic vocabulary' (also the source of the SHAPE coding method). A labelled vocabulary seems to matter.

source: Hembree (1992) Experiments and relational studies in problem solving: a meta-analysis (Journal for Research in Mathematics Education 23(3), 242-273)
finding: The largest synthesis of the heuristics-teaching literature: 487 reports. Heuristic instruction was not better in early grades (K to 5), mildly better in middle grades (6 to 8), and distinctly better in high school. Training in drawing diagrams, figures or sketches gave the largest single performance gain. Teachers trained in heuristic methods raised student performance.
numbers: 487 reports integrated. Abstract gives direction and ranking only; effect sizes were not available to me.
limits: Only the abstract (via Crossref and OpenAlex) was read; the effect sizes and moderator tables in the full paper were not opened. Pre-1992 studies on humans, mixed designs and measures.
agent_relevance: Two usable points. (1) Heuristic benefit grows with the solver's competence (nothing in early grades, strong in high school), parallel to G12: search and heuristics lift only where there is a foothold. (2) Making a figure or representation is the best-supported heuristic, which supports O6 (change representation) as the first operator to try.

source: Anonymous authors (2025) SMART: Self-generating and self-validating multi-dimensional assessment for LLMs' mathematical problem solving (arXiv 2505.16646), benchmark built on Polya's four steps
finding: Splits each maths problem into four Polya-aligned tasks (Understanding, Reasoning as a symbolic formalisation, Arithmetic, Reflection and Refinement) and tests 22 models. Understanding is mostly solved; reasoning and reflection vary hugely; final-answer accuracy hides weaknesses. The strict 'all four pass' score is much lower than answer accuracy.
numbers: Most models score above 90% on Understanding. Reasoning accuracy ranges from 9.05% to 93.61%. Best Reflection score 78.62%, about nine times the weakest. o3: final answer 91.44% but All-Pass only 64.87%. o4-mini 93.75% vs Claude 3.7 Sonnet 93.53% final accuracy but Reasoning 90.72% vs 74.18%. GPT-4.1: Reasoning 73.29%, Arithmetic 45.71% vs o4-mini 90.72% and 98.25%. With perturbations, irrelevant noise hurts Reasoning most (GPT-4.1 drop 26.75%, Claude 3.7 8.37%); changed operations or numbers hurt Arithmetic most. A reflection-and-refinement prompt aimed at the weakest dimension raised Qwen2.5-72B final accuracy by 11.77%; Llama3.1-8B dropped slightly.
limits: Task design (injected rule-based errors, SMT-LIB formalisation) is the authors' operationalisation, not Polya's own method. Tasks are separate prompts, not one running solution. Comments on arXiv ask for more data or method fixes. Dimension scores for open models vary with how well they handle the SMT-LIB output format.
agent_relevance: Confirms the Polya-step split (understand, plan, execute, look back) is measurable in LLMs and that failures are not uniform: poor models fail at reasoning/arithmetic, strong ones at reflection. Supports using counted execution checks (code) for the arithmetic step and treating self-reflection as the weakest component (matches G2, 4b).

source: Schoenfeld (1992) Learning to think mathematically, comment on school drills and on schemas versus strategies
finding: Competing explanation for expert success: stored problem schemas (recognise features, use procedure) rather than general heuristics. Schoenfeld argues experts use schemas for familiar problems and strategies only beyond the routine, and that relying on crude schemas ('when you see these features, use this procedure') gives error-prone, easily forgotten performance.
numbers: None.
limits: Argument (chess players and mathematicians as examples; Mayer 1985 and Sowder 1985 cited for caution), not a test. The education community's caution about schema-only teaching shapes his tone.
agent_relevance: Two routes in S0/S1: retrieve a known procedure if the problem class matches (schema), else use an operator (heuristic) at impasse. Our gate already separates these; the evidence says do not expect heuristics to help on routine problems.
